prompt: You average increasingly many independent identically distributed measurements with finite nonzero variance. What does the central limit theorem support?

options.text: A normal limit for the centred and scaled average.
options.explanation: The theorem describes that standardised sampling distribution as sample size grows.

options.text: Each original measurement becomes normally distributed.
options.explanation: Averaging does not change the original population law.

options.text: Any sample of thirty guarantees accurate extreme tails.
options.explanation: No universal finite sample threshold supplies that guarantee.

options.text: The standard deviation of the average grows in proportion to sample size.
options.explanation: Under these assumptions it shrinks with the square root of sample size.

workedExample: Identify what is repeated: whole samples and their averages. Centre and scale those averages before discussing a normal limit. Check finite-sample accuracy separately, especially in the tails.

link.title: Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell

prompt: An engineer derives a high latency percentile from only the mean and standard deviation by assuming a normal model. Which criticisms are valid? Select all that apply.

options.text: A normal model permits negative values, so it is only an approximation to latency.
options.explanation: Assess whether the resulting negative mass and tail fit are acceptable.

options.text: The 99.7% three-standard-deviation rule is a two-sided band.
options.explanation: Its upper edge is at a different one-sided percentile.

options.text: Nonnegative data must have a heavy tail.
options.explanation: Nonnegativity implies neither heavy tails nor right skew.

options.text: Mean and standard deviation do not determine arbitrary distribution tails.
options.explanation: Different distributions can share these summaries but have different percentiles.

workedExample: Challenge the distributional assumption before interpreting the arithmetic. Measure enough tail observations or use an appropriate histogram, and separate two-sided coverage from a one-sided percentile.
